title: Secrets, variables, environments and deployments
summary: Workflows need credentials to deploy, publish and call services. Secrets store them encrypted, environments decide which jobs may use them and who must approve, and the `permissions` key keeps the built-in token on a short leash.
outcomes: Choose between a secret and a variable, and between repository, environment and organization level
Read a secret in a workflow without leaking it into logs or scripts
Gate a deployment behind an environment with required reviewers
Explain why OpenID Connect is safer than a stored cloud key
Predict when a workflow will not receive secrets at all

lenses.everyday: A hotel gives the cleaning crew key cards, not the master key ring. Each card opens only the floors on that person's sheet, only during the shift, and stops working at the end of the day. Opening the safe at the front desk needs a manager present. Nobody writes door codes on the whiteboard. Secrets are the cards, environments are the manager-present rule for the valuable rooms, and the built-in token is a card that expires when the shift ends.
lenses.legal: Client trust account credentials are not emailed around the firm. They sit with a custodian, access is limited to named roles, disbursements above a threshold need a second approver, and every use is logged. The mapping is direct. Secrets are held by the platform and never shown again after entry. Environments restrict which jobs may draw on them. Required reviewers are dual authorization. The deployment history is the ledger. Least privilege is the same principle as need-to-know: a workflow that only reads code should hold nothing that can write.
lenses.ml: Your training workflow needs a token for the experiment tracker and a key for the bucket that holds checkpoints. Hard-coding them in `train.py` leaks them to everyone who can read the repository, and to the internet if it is public. Stored as secrets, they are injected as environment variables only into the step that needs them. Put the bucket key in a `production` environment and only runs from `main`, approved by you, can write to the bucket that holds the released checkpoints.
lenses.technical: Secrets are encrypted values exposed to workflows through the `secrets` context. Variables are plain-text configuration exposed through `vars`. Both exist at organization, repository and environment level, and the most specific level wins. A job that declares an `environment` must satisfy that environment's protection rules before it starts, and only then receives its secrets. `GITHUB_TOKEN` is scoped per job by the `permissions` key. With OpenID Connect, a job exchanges a short-lived signed identity token for cloud credentials, so no long-lived cloud key is stored anywhere.

sections.heading: Secret or variable, and at which level

items.title: Secret
points: Encrypted, and cannot be read back after you save it
Masked in logs when printed exactly as stored
For API keys, tokens, passwords and signing keys

items.title: Variable
points: Plain text, visible to anyone who can see the settings
For names, addresses, feature switches and region codes

head: Level
Where you set it
Use it for
rows: Organization settings, with a list of repositories allowed to use it
Most things in a single project
Anything that touches production or costs money

blocks.text: When the same name exists at more than one level, the most specific one wins: environment over repository, repository over organization. That lets `TRACKER_URL` point at a test server by default and at the real one only for jobs in the `production` environment.

blocks.prompt: Someone opens a pull request from a fork that edits your workflow to print `secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN`. The workflow triggers on `pull_request`. What gets printed?
blocks.answer: Nothing useful. A workflow triggered by a pull request from a fork does not receive secrets, and its `GITHUB_TOKEN` is read-only. The value is empty. That default is what makes it safe to run CI on strangers' contributions. The `pull_request_target` event changes these rules and is dangerous for that reason. [Actions at scale](#expert-actions-architecture) explains why.

blocks.title: Three separate stores
blocks.text: Actions secrets are only for Actions. Dependabot has its own secrets, used when its pull requests trigger workflows or need a private registry. Codespaces has another set, injected into your development environment. A secret saved in one store is invisible to the other two.

sections.heading: Using a secret without leaking it

blocks.code:
name: Publish metrics

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  publish:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Confirm the token is set without showing it
        env:
          TRACKER_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.TRACKER_TOKEN }}
        run: |
          if [ -z "$TRACKER_TOKEN" ]; then
            echo "TRACKER_TOKEN is empty"
            exit 1
          fi
          echo "TRACKER_TOKEN is set"

      - name: Upload evaluation metrics
        env:
          TRACKER_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.TRACKER_TOKEN }}
          TRACKER_URL: ${{ vars.TRACKER_URL }}
        run: python scripts/upload_metrics.py --url "$TRACKER_URL"
blocks.caption: The secret enters single steps as an environment variable. The script reads it from the environment.

items: **Scope to the step.** Put `env` on the step that needs the secret, not on the whole workflow.
**Never build a command line from a secret.** Pass it through the environment and let the program read it. Command lines show up in process lists and logs.
**Do not print, and do not transform.** GitHub masks the exact stored value in logs. A base64-encoded or sliced copy is a different string and is not masked.
**Avoid structured secrets.** A JSON document stored as one secret masks poorly. Store each sensitive value separately.
**Secrets cannot be used directly in `if`.** Copy the secret into `env` and test the variable, as the first step above does.
**Rotate.** A key that has lived for three years has been within reach of everyone who ever had access. Replace long-lived keys on a schedule.

blocks.title: Masking catches accidents and nothing else
blocks.text: Log masking catches accidents. It does not stop a step from sending a secret somewhere on purpose. Anyone who can change a workflow that receives a secret can read that secret. Control who can change workflows on branches that get secrets, and review workflow changes like any other code.

sections.heading: Environments: a gate in front of the valuable things

blocks.text: An environment is a named deployment target, such as `staging` or `production`, with its own secrets, variables and protection rules. A job opts in with one key. Until the rules are satisfied, the job does not start and cannot see the environment's secrets.

blocks.code:
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - run: python tools/build.py

  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: production
      url: https://example.org
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - name: Deploy
        env:
          DEPLOY_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN }}
        run: ./scripts/deploy.sh
blocks.caption: The deploy job waits for the production environment's rules before it starts

head: Protection rule
Effect
rows: The job pauses until a listed person approves it on the run page
The job waits a set number of minutes before starting
Only runs from the listed branches or tags may use the environment

blocks.text: Every job that targets an environment creates a deployment record. The repository's **Deployments** page shows what was deployed where, from which commit, and who approved it. This guide's own workflow uses an environment named `github-pages` for that reason. Environments exist on public repositories on every plan. Protection rules on private repositories depend on your plan.

sections.heading: The built-in token and least privilege

blocks.text: Every job gets a `GITHUB_TOKEN`. The `permissions` key decides what it can do. The moment you list one permission, every permission you did not list becomes `none`, so a short list is a strong statement. A job-level block replaces the workflow-level one for that job.

blocks.code:
name: Comment on pull requests

on:
  pull_request:

permissions:
  contents: read             # default for every job in this file

jobs:
  comment:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      pull-requests: write   # this job alone may comment
    steps:
      - name: Leave a note
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          GH_REPO: ${{ github.repository }}
          PR_NUMBER: ${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
        run: gh pr comment "$PR_NUMBER" --body "Smoke test started."

blocks.title: Set the default to read-only
blocks.text: Repository settings include a default for workflow permissions under **Settings**, **Actions**, **General**. Choose the read-only option. Workflows that need more will say so in their own `permissions` block, where a reviewer can see it. On pull requests from forks the token stays read-only whatever the workflow asks for.

sections.heading: OpenID Connect: no stored cloud key

blocks.text: The classic way to let a workflow reach a cloud account is to create an access key in the cloud console and paste it into a secret. That key works from anywhere, for anyone who holds it, until someone remembers to rotate it. OpenID Connect, usually shortened to OIDC, removes the stored key.

steps.label: GitHub signs an identity token
steps.note: It states the repository, branch, workflow and environment

steps.label: Cloud checks its trust policy
steps.note: Only this repository and branch are accepted

steps.label: Short-lived credentials
steps.note: Valid for minutes, for this job only

blocks.caption: Nothing long-lived is stored on either side

blocks.text: You configure trust once on the cloud side: accept tokens from GitHub, but only when the token says the run came from this repository, this branch or this environment. Each major cloud provider publishes an official action that performs the exchange. The concept is the same everywhere.

blocks.title: Dual authorization and the audit trail
blocks.text: Required reviewers on a production environment are dual authorization: the person who wrote the change is not the only person who can release it. The deployment record shows the approver, the time and the exact commit. If your work is subject to change-management requirements, this is the evidence, and it is produced as a side effect of working normally.

blocks.title: Approvals reach you where you are
blocks.text: A pending deployment review sends a notification and can be approved from the run page in a phone browser. If long focused sessions at a desk are hard to guarantee, a review gate you can clear from anywhere is more dependable than one that needs you at the keyboard at the moment the build finishes.

howto.task: Add a secret and use it in a workflow
browser: On the **Secrets** tab select **New repository secret**. Enter a name in capitals with underscores, such as `TRACKER_TOKEN`, paste the value, and save.
On the **Variables** tab add non-sensitive settings such as `TRACKER_URL`.
In the workflow, map the secret into `env` on the step that needs it, as in this lesson's example.
Run the workflow and confirm the step works. If the value is printed anywhere, the log shows `***` in its place.
phone: Repository secrets cannot be managed in GitHub Mobile as of this writing.
In the mobile browser, open the repository's **Settings** on the desktop site and follow the browser steps. Paste the value from a password manager instead of typing it.
Avoid handling production credentials on a phone in public. A secret someone read over your shoulder must be rotated like any other leak.
cli: `gh secret set TRACKER_TOKEN` prompts for the value without showing it. Do not put the value on the command line, where shell history keeps it.
`gh variable set TRACKER_URL --body "https://tracker.example.org"` for plain configuration.
`gh secret list` and `gh variable list` show names and update times. Secret values are never shown.
`gh secret set DEPLOY_TOKEN --env production` stores a secret on an environment.
Edit the workflow to read the secret through `env`, commit and push.
editor: Edit the workflow file in VS Code or a codespace. The GitHub Actions extension can suggest the secret and variable names it knows about.
Use the integrated terminal for `gh secret set`, so the value never lands in a file.
Keep real values out of the workspace. A `.env` file belongs in `.gitignore`.
Never paste a secret value into a chat with a coding agent. Ask the agent to write code that reads the value from the environment, and set the value yourself.

howto.task: Gate a deployment behind an approval
browser: Open **Settings**, then **Environments**, and select **New environment**. Name it `production`.
Turn on **Required reviewers** and add yourself or a teammate.
Under deployment branches and tags, limit the environment to the default branch.
Add the deployment secret to this environment, not to the repository.
Add `environment: production` to the deploy job and push.
When the run reaches that job it pauses. Open the run, select **Review deployments**, tick the environment, and approve.
phone: Create the environment on a computer, or in the mobile browser on the desktop site.
When a run is waiting, the pending review shows on the run page. As of this writing GitHub Mobile also surfaces deployment reviews, so you can often approve from the notification.
Read which commit you are approving before you tap. The approval is recorded under your name.
cli: Environments are created in the browser, or with `gh api` against the repository's environments endpoint.
`gh secret set DEPLOY_TOKEN --env production` adds the environment secret.
`gh run list --workflow deploy.yml` shows the runs. One that is waiting for review has the status `waiting`.
`gh run view <run-id> --web` opens the run page, where you approve the deployment.
editor: Add `environment: production` to the deploy job in the workflow file and commit.
The GitHub Actions extension shows the run as waiting once it reaches the gate.
Approve in the browser. The approval is deliberately a human step outside the editor.
Do not give a coding agent the ability to approve deployments. The gate exists so that a person decides.

pitfalls.trap: Committing a credential to the repository because adding a secret felt like too many steps.
pitfalls.fix: Treat anything committed as public. Store it as a secret and read it from the environment. If it was committed, rotate it first and clean up second.

pitfalls.trap: Printing a secret to debug it and relying on masking to hide it.
pitfalls.fix: Check that a secret is set without showing it: test whether the variable is empty and print only a yes or a no.

pitfalls.trap: Storing a deployment key at repository level, where any workflow on any branch can read it.
pitfalls.fix: Move it to an environment that is restricted to the default branch and protected by a reviewer.

pitfalls.trap: Leaving the default token permissions at read and write for every workflow.
pitfalls.fix: Set the repository default to read-only and declare `permissions` in each workflow.

pitfalls.trap: Expecting Actions secrets in a workflow triggered by a Dependabot pull request. They are not provided, and the job fails in a confusing way.
pitfalls.fix: Add the same value as a Dependabot secret if the job truly needs it, or let that job skip for Dependabot.

quiz.q: `API_URL` is defined as a repository variable and again on the `production` environment. A job declares `environment: production`. Which value does `vars.API_URL` return?
choices: The environment value
The repository value
Both, joined with a comma
An error, because the names clash
quiz.why: The most specific level wins: environment over repository over organization. Jobs that do not declare the environment still get the repository value.

quiz.q: A step runs `echo "$TOKEN" | base64`, where `TOKEN` comes from a secret. What appears in the log?
choices: `***`, because every form of a secret is masked
Nothing, because the step is blocked
The base64 text, unmasked
The original secret in plain text
quiz.why: Masking matches the exact stored value. An encoded copy is a different string, so it is printed, and base64 is trivially reversible. This is why you never print or transform secrets in a workflow.

quiz.q: A workflow's top-level `permissions` block contains only `contents: read`. What can a job's token do with pull requests?
choices: Read and write, which is the default
Read only
Whatever the repository default says
Nothing, because unlisted permissions become none
quiz.why: Listing any permission switches every unlisted one off. That is the feature: the workflow file states the complete set. A job that must comment on pull requests adds `pull-requests: write` explicitly.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of OpenID Connect over storing a cloud access key as a secret?
choices: It is faster than reading a secret
No long-lived credential exists to leak; each job gets short-lived access tied to its repository and branch
It works without any configuration in the cloud account
It lets pull requests from forks deploy safely
quiz.why: With OIDC the cloud issues temporary credentials only after verifying a signed token that describes the run. There is nothing permanent to steal or rotate. It does need a trust policy configured once on the cloud side.

quiz.q: A deploy job declares `environment: production`, which has a required reviewer. When can the job read the environment's secrets?
choices: As soon as the workflow starts
Only after a reviewer approves and the job starts
Never; environment secrets are for display only
Only when the workflow is triggered by hand
quiz.why: The job is held before it starts, and environment secrets are released only to a job that has passed the protection rules. An unapproved run never sees them.

mission.title: Store a secret, gate a job, shrink the token
mission.where: Your own repository, using a made-up value. No real credential is needed.
steps: Create a repository secret named `PRACTICE_TOKEN` with any made-up value, and a variable named `PRACTICE_URL`.
Write a workflow whose one step maps both into `env` and prints only whether `PRACTICE_TOKEN` is non-empty. Run it and read the log.
Add a line that echoes the secret itself. Confirm the log shows `***`, then remove the line.
Create an environment named `practice-prod` with yourself as required reviewer, and add `environment: practice-prod` to the job.
Run the workflow again, watch it wait, and approve it from the run page. Find the record on the **Deployments** page.
Make sure the workflow has a `permissions` block containing only `contents: read`, and set the repository's default workflow permissions to read-only.
Delete the practice secret and the environment when you are done.

terms.def: An encrypted value stored by GitHub and exposed to workflows through the `secrets` context. It cannot be read back after saving.
A plain-text configuration value exposed to workflows through the `vars` context.
A named deployment target with its own secrets, variables and protection rules that a job must satisfy before it runs.
A person or team who must approve a job before it can use a protected environment.
Granting a credential only the access the task needs, so a mistake or a leak can do limited damage.
A standard that lets a job prove its identity with a short-lived signed token and receive temporary cloud credentials in exchange.
GitHub's replacement of exact secret values in workflow logs with asterisks. It does not cover transformed copies.
A record that a job targeted an environment, including the commit, the time, the result and any approver.

commands.does: Creates or updates a repository secret, prompting for the value so it stays out of shell history.
Stores the secret on an environment, so only jobs that pass its rules can read it.
Lists secret names and when each was last updated. Values are never shown.
Creates or updates a plain-text configuration variable.
Lists configuration variables with their values.
Removes a secret. Workflows that read it will receive an empty value.
Opens a run in the browser, where pending deployment reviews are approved.
